content.body: Have you ever needed to find the first letter in a word that doesn't repeat? That's exactly what we'll learn to do efficiently. We'll discover how to track what we've seen using a clever lookup technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Identify the first unique character in a string.
2. Implement a hash map to remember character counts.
3. Explain why checking a lookup is faster than re-scanning.
4. Determine when to store vs. check values in the map.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: In the word 'hello', which letter appears first without repeating?
content.successMessage: Great! 'h' is the first letter that doesn't repeat.

content.title: Try a longer word
content.prompt: In 'aabbccde', which is the first unique character?
content.successMessage: Nice! 'd' is the first character that appears only once.

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Well done! You scanned through the letters to find none are unique here.

content.body: You just performed a brute force check: for each character, you looked through the rest of the string to see if it repeats. This works but becomes slow with longer strings.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Imagine a string with 10,000 characters. Checking each character against all others takes too long. We need a smarter way. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-scanning the string, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to note each character we encounter. This lets us check in one step whether we've seen something before.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down every character we see. When we encounter a new character, we check the notebook first instead of searching through the whole string again.

content.body: We'll make one pass through the string, using a hash map to count how many times each character appears. Then we'll make a second pass to find the first character with a count of 1.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample: For 'leetcode': First pass counts: l→1, e→2, t→1, c→1, o→1, d→1. Second pass: 'l' has count 1 → return index 0.

content.body:
1. Create an empty object to store character counts.
2. Loop through the string once, adding each character to the object with its count.
3. Loop through the string again, checking each character's count in the object.
4. Return the index of the first character with count 1, or -1 if none.

steps.instruction: Add a second loop through the string. Check each character's count in charCount. Return the index of the first character with count 1. If none found, return -1.

content.body: Great work! You've learned how to find the first unique character by remembering what you've seen in a hash map. Key takeaways: store characters as keys and counts as values, check the map during the second pass, and this approach is much faster than re-scanning the whole string repeatedly.
